posts.text:
$NVDA If you are wondering why the stock is down today despite reporting a beat and raise quarter here is my 2 cents. 

✅They didn’t file their 10q at the same time as earnings release as was their custom. Red Flag 🚩 

✅The call and Q&A didn’t address investor concerns. They claimed zero sales to China. That is laughable. 

✅After call very large holders of stock get to talk to management. They ask tougher questions than sell side. Collectively they likely didn’t like the answers or legal speak non answers. In short they don’t believe the future guidance is real. The pop in the morning was sold and continues as of this post. This is called a long squeeze…opposite of short squeeze. 

Bottom line: The market is worried that the former CFO and Board are in CYA mode on the China question and reported Jensen’s numbers and guidance but didn’t file 10q and sign off on them legally yet. Speculation is that they will open the kimono on China numbers after an investigation and pretend they didn’t know. 

Additionally the other problems for the stock are: 

-competition will take advantage of leadership disruption and gross margins will eventually go lower. 
-Neo clouds are having trouble getting financing to buy more chips. 
-The DSOs of receivables went to 64 from 60 last Q and 45 prior. Customers are taking longer to pay essentially. 
-SEC investigation and DOJ investigation overhang
-And finally macro concerns that the credit markets are questioning the build out of AI and the cycle has turned down. 

Basically The market doesn’t believe the forward forecasts.

$Tencent / Chinese CSPs’ tone on the AI capex cycle is very clear - 

Martin Lau laid out a clear case for why AI capex should moderate after 2027:

1/ Front-loaded investment: AI infrastructure is like building a factory. Once built, it can continuously train new models and generate tokens.

2/ Lower hardware costs: The same equipment should cost significantly less by 2028.

3/ Rapid efficiency gains: The same infrastructure can deliver exponentially more training compute and token output over time.

Takeaway: Martin is effectively calling for a peak in AI capex in 2026-27, with a meaningful decline in capex intensity thereafter, even as AI demand continues to grow.

The read-through for semis is interesting: If annual industry AI capex eventually normalizes below $1T, assigning a mid-range multiple to normalized earnings, that’s your industry total size.

quoted.text:
Why I am not investing in the Anthropic IPO.

$ANT 

- Range of outcomes is extremely wide
- Risk/reward is negatively asymmetric
- Business relies on regulatory climate to exist
- AI/Technology moves extremely fast, risk of disruption is extremely high
- User patterns and AI utility is still early days - we literally don’t know where this is going
- This is the exact opposite of “slow change”
- And just because people use Claude Code today does not mean they won’t use Francois Code tomorrow
- Many are trying to understand real unit economics using current financial reports: I think that’s futile right now
- Founders have voting control of the company
- Raising capital on extremely speculative and hype things like curing cancer using AI etc.
- Investing in business is not the same as “investing in innovation”
- Competitive climate is crazy. Everything is up in the air
- Anthropic needs the distributions (and compute infrastructure) of other companies (competitors) to sell their own models (e.g. Amazon). 
- Fragility and conflicts of interest.
- Huge cash balance is not enough to make me want to invest in this company
- Their future commitments are huge, the mismatch is huge and makes any calculations very speculative
- Creative destruction. Race to the bottom. Tit-for-tat war between the top players in Big Tech/AI
- AI could succeed massively as a technology and Anthropic could still fail
- Anthropic could succeed spectacularly, and Anthropic shareholders could still lose big

posts.text:
SK Hynix -- over the past month, the sell side analysts have increased their 2027 revenue growth estimates from +45% to +60% and their 2027 eps growth estimates from +30% to +50%

During this same time frame SK Hynix ($000660.ks) is down -25% and now trades at 2.12x 2027 EPS using these new sell side eps estimates.

My base case model has revenue growth at 65-70% in 2027 however my eps growth is much higher because of the stock buybacks which the sell side isn't accounting for in their estimates. 

Assuming SK Hynix buys back 3.2% to 3.5% of the outstanding shares every quarter from 2026 Q4 through 2027 Q4, then 65-70% revenue growth in 2027 looks like 80-90% eps growth in 2027... in which case SK Hynix is trading today at 1.7x 2027 eps 

It's pretty rare to see estimates getting increased this much while a stock is falling... just another sign of the massive dislocation we're seeing in the market between fundamentals and valuations.

posts.name: Cheddar Flow
posts.text:
$NVDA earnings summary:

Q3 revenue hit $115.8B, crushing the $109.3B estimate and topping even the highest analyst forecast of $114.9B. Adjusted EPS came in at $2.68 vs. $2.47 expected, with a 74.9% gross margin. That makes 17 straight quarters beating consensus and 15 straight above the top of Nvidia's own guidance. 

Data center did the heavy lifting at $107.6B (est. $101.9B), split between hyperscalers ($60.1B) and AI clouds, industrial & enterprise ($47.5B), with Vera Rubin alone adding nearly $20B quarter over quarter. Compute & networking ($106.0B), graphics ($9.8B) and edge computing ($8.2B) all came in ahead of estimates too.

The outlook is just as strong. Nvidia guided Q4 revenue to $127.4B–$132.6B (~$130B midpoint) vs. $125.3B expected, with 71–72% gross margins and about $10.7B in operating expenses. That guide assumes zero China data center revenue, even after $2.4B in Hopper shipments there this quarter. Commitments jumped to $390B from $279B in Q2, neocloud agreements total $32B, and the board added $150B to the buyback, leaving $227.3B to deploy through FY2028. The AI build-out isn't slowing down.

THE LEADERSHIP CHANGE:

On November 12 the board announced that Huang resigned as President, CEO and director, effective immediately. That came four days after the board opened an independent investigation into his conduct.

CFO Colette Kress is interim CEO and remains CFO. Harvey Jones becomes the first Chair of the Board in the company's history. The board will consider internal and external candidates.

The board's only operating statement: it expects "operations, customer commitments and product roadmap to continue without interruption." The report and the call stay on schedule.

The results are already locked. The quarter ended before the leadership news.

NVIDIA has beaten EPS 12 of the last 12 quarters by an average of 7.6%. It has beaten revenue 12 of 12, by 3.5% on average over the last four.

Grosse journée sur la TECH

Je vous ait résumé ce qu'il s'est dit lors du premier jour de TomorrowX :

1. AMD : Lisa Su dit que la demande dépasse l'offre malgré les contrôles à l'export. Elle parle d'un cycle générationnel plutôt que cyclique, sans phase de digestion, même si le ROI revient dans chaque discussion avec les clients. La salle a trouvé qu'elle n'avait pas dit grand-chose de nouveau.

2. SpaceX et Anthropic : le CFO de SpaceX, a priori, n'est pas inquiet sur la demande de compute et pense qu'Anthropic en aura besoin de beaucoup plus. Pour financer 10 GW, il n'y aurait pas besoin de lever des fonds propres : le cash-flow et la dette suffiraient. Beaucoup y ont vu le talk le plus intéressant de la journée. Le bémol : quand on annonce plus de demande, le marché ne monte plus, il pose des questions sur le financement. En face, Gerstner a surtout fait la promo d'Anthropic, tout en estimant qu'environ 500 MW d'inférence pourraient lui suffire l'an prochain.

3. Druckenmiller : il est en mode préservation du capital, ni long ni short actions, et juge le marché un peu survendu. Il voit Warsh plus hawkish que prévu, des spreads de crédit écartés et un second semestre 2027 potentiellement négatif pour l'économie. Pour lui, les infrastructures ne sont qu'un trade tactique : la valeur viendra des usages comme la santé et la cyber, avec des labs qui vendront des tâches plutôt que des tokens.

4. Un peu de signal : Vercel est passé d'environ 600 M$ d'ARR début octobre à environ 700 M$, soit +100 M$ en cinq semaines grâce au code agentique. Le CEO de Fireworks cherche toujours du compute et voit encore une forte pénurie. Cerebras dément tout froid avec OpenAI et attend une hausse du CA du T3 au T4, puis en 2027. Michael Dell ne change pas d'avis sur le buildout.

5. Le camp bear : Gavin Baker vendrait MU et plus largement le groupe capex. Plusieurs participants pensent que les profits glissent vers les labs d'IA, et que les infrastructures et les semis deviennent la commodité, puisque c'est la relation avec l'utilisateur qui compte. La salle était à moitié vide, ce que certains lisent comme le signe que le point bas n'est pas encore fait

Compliqué de se positionner ici, je pense que les signaux sont brouillés, on sent clairement que le sentiment est mauvais 

On a l'impression que toutes les caisses ont été vidé pour aller sur Anthropic et que tout le monde attend ce soir, le juge de paix $NVDA

$SLS Regardless of if you know anything about science and statistics, I feel like everyone should ask the following question and use their gut instinct/common sense to try to understand the answer:

Why was this the shortest conference call I can recall ever for a successful clinical trial? Let alone one that is apparently transformative? The start of the section after forward looking statements was at the 1:18 mark and ended at 5:00. The remaining ~10 minutes was self-congratulations. That's 15 minutes in total. For context, $ABVX had a nearly 50-minute call to discuss their original induction data. The average call is between 30 and 75+ minutes post pivotal data.

The $SLS call was:

1) Here is the data in slide format and basics on trial design (essentially just the press release granularity) (~3 minutes 40 seconds).

2) Thank you everyone for supporting us, it's been such a long road to get to this point (~10 minutes)

3) Goodbye. (5 seconds)

This was the single pivotal moment where, as management said themselves, they've been slogging at for over a decade. This is also a way to directly (and legally) promote to KOLs, investors, etc about why this is so transformative, your opinion on market opportunity, the timelines to submit, and strategic interest color. Why would you spend as little time as possible on the call?

Does that make any sense, at all? What would be the motives for not wanting to talk about it any further, or not wanting to take any questions from analysts who were primed to also congratulate you and give you very softball questions?

I don't think management is clueless. Their past fireside chats were 20-30 minutes each. Is it possible that they thought the risks of saying anything more than what was on the slides, or of being asked a question that would put them into a challenging position, was not worth the reward of saying anything further about the trial, the drug, the opportunity, or their strategic goals?

posts.name: Bill Ackman
posts.text:
I believe the @nvidia board is not acting in the best interest of shareholders nor in a manner consistent with their fiduciary duties. 

What we know is that the board fired Jensen or forced his resignation for violating company policy and/or in response to the accusation of an affair with a spy. 

They did so without careful consideration of the impact on the company, its customers, its shareholders or other stakeholders. 

They rushed to judgment without the benefit of careful due diligence or even with a basic understanding of the facts. 

How do we know this? 

We know this by how quickly Jensen was fired and how little was known at the time of his firing. 

It takes time to convene a board meeting.  There was time, maybe, for one Zoom. 

And this is a decision that should have been made by a board sitting in person and carefully deliberating the facts once they are known.  

And they should have slept on the decision and met again the day after to discuss the facts, the risks and the other implications of their decision. 

The timing and lack of information did not allow for careful board deliberation. 

While boards can fire a CEO for an inappropriate relationship with a subordinate, it should not be an automatic decision. That is why we have boards comprised of humans and not agents. 

A board should consider whether or not such a relationship was consensual or whether it was an abuse of power dynamics. And a board has to consider what the impact of the firing is on all stakeholders. 

If I were in this board, I would not have rushed to judgment based on articles in the media. I would have made sure the board had all of the facts so it could make a careful and informed decision. 

Boards of Delaware companies have a duty of care which means they must make informed, prudent and good faith decisions. This clearly did not happen here. 

What law firm is advising this board?  

Or is the board even taken good legal advice? 

It doesn’t look like it. 

And now the board is compounding its failures by insisting that there is no possibility for Jensen’s return as CEO. 

Why is it in the best interest of the company to foreclose the possibility of Jensen’s return and to do so before all of the facts are known? This is yet another breach of their duty of care. 

Furthermore, the board has launched an investigation whose scope is unknown. Investigations can be extremely damaging to a company and should be carefully targeted to address whatever facts need to be known rather than be overly broad in scope. 

In short, this looks like a series of major governance failures by directors that panicked due to headlines in the media. They likely felt compelled to do something because they were afraid of looking bad in the media, not because it was the right thing for them company. 

They couldn’t stand the heat. 

The board’s conduct here is shocking for a company of this scale and importance to our country and the world at large, particularly at this moment in history.

This chart overlays the current decline in Nasdaq-100 futures against four historical selloffs, lined up at the peak:

posts.name: Cullen Roche
posts.text:
Fair point that reserves settle between the state and the private sector too. And if you mean hierarchy in the finality sense, I agree reserves sit higher. They’re the settlement asset.

Where I disagree is the “claim on state money” part. Go read an actual deposit agreement. Bank of America’s 2026 agreement says they can restrict, delay, question or refuse cash withdrawals, and if they close your account they can mail you a check. That’s not a promise to deliver state money. It’s a dollar denominated debt that the bank settles however it chooses, usually by moving you to another bank. The FDIC works the same way. It guarantees par in the unit of account, not delivery of currency. You don't have a claim on "state money" and households can't make a bank give them state money because the bank's liability isn't state money, it's BANK MONEY. 

So deposits are settled in state money, but they aren’t claims on it. And they aren’t derivatives either. Banks create the deposit first and the Fed supplies reserves to accommodate it. The causality runs from deposits to reserves, not the other way around. 

The entire Federal Reserve system exists to service deposits. That's literally why it was created in 1913 - to service interbank deposit transfers. But MMT took the whole mechanism and created this misleading narrative by which the reserve system can be depicted as the start of the monetary system when it is factually secondary.

posts.name: Michael A. Arouet
posts.text:
Gold is trading near $3,750/oz, its lowest in over a year and down more than 30% from the January peak. Let’s take a look what’s driving that, shall we?

Here are the main reasons for the drop:

• Hawkish Fed signals have markets pricing a near-certain December rate hike, raising the opportunity cost of holding non-yielding gold.

• A strong US dollar (near 19-month highs) and elevated real yields (~3% on TIPS, with 10-year yields around 5%) make yield-bearing assets far more attractive.

• Some selling is positioning-driven as investors raise cash amid broader market volatility.

• Geopolitical tensions have lifted oil and inflation, reinforcing rate-hike bets rather than boosting safe-haven demand.

• Technical breaks below key levels have accelerated the decline.

What’s the mid-term outlook then?

• Near-term pressure is likely to persist while the Fed remains hawkish.

• Banks have cut targets but still expect recovery: Goldman sees ~$4,150 by end-2026 and ~$4,650–$4,800 by end-2027, UBS targets $4,500 by end-2026 and $5,000 by end-2027.

• Central bank buying, resilient ETF holdings, and concerns over debt and fiscal sustainability continue to provide a floor.

• Meaningful upside is more likely once the hiking cycle ends and cuts are priced (expected later in 2027), drawing private and Western ETF demand back in.

Overall, this appears to be a rates-driven correction rather than a structural breakdown, medium-term bias remains constructive on dips for longer-term holders. What do you think folks?

Is encrypted data just a locked vault waiting to be cracked?

Digital Asset CEO Yuval Rooz says encrypted data could eventually be cracked, so Canton shares transaction data only with the parties involved, not across the network

"We don't have a centralized privacy solution. The privacy is by actually segregating the account. So your node on Canton will only have your smart contracts. My node will not even know that Scott's smart contracts exist."

"Most chains, because they fully replicate the data, are trying to come up with an encryption that says, there's data here, but I just don't know what it is."

"Canton says, no. I don't even want you to have the data on your node. It's not your business to know that it exists."

"Any hacker steals a lot of encrypted data. Think about it like you're stealing a vault. You just don't know how to open it yet. But you know that there's something inside, and you're going to invest a lot of resources to open that vault eventually."

"So our view is, don't even put Scott's vault in my infrastructure. Don't replicate the data all over the chain. That's a very big design decision between us and others."

DANSKE BANK ADDS THIRD FED RATE HIKE, SEES RATES AT 4.50%–4.75% BY MARCH 2027

Danske Bank has revised its Federal Reserve outlook, adding another rate increase to its forecast.

The bank now expects three additional hikes, bringing the federal funds target range to 4.50%–4.75% by March 2027.

Analysts cite growing inflation concerns among Fed policymakers, despite limited monetary policy guidance from Fed Chair Kevin Warsh.

Danske expects stronger underlying economic growth to sustain inflationary pressures, forcing further tightening.

The revised forecast reinforces expectations of higher borrowing costs for longer.

HIGHER INTEREST RATES THREATEN CREDIT MARKETS AS PRIVATE LENDING DEMAND RISES

Rising borrowing costs could push more companies away from public debt markets and toward private credit, according to executives at Bloomberg's Global Credit Forum.

KKR warns that distressed debt ratios in U.S. and European leveraged loans and high-yield bonds could climb to 8%–9%, signaling mounting financial pressure.

Meanwhile, HSBC identifies private credit as a major vulnerability, particularly loans issued to highly leveraged middle-market companies.

Persistent rate hikes and AI-driven disruption could accelerate defaults, restructurings and broader credit-market stress.

FED'S WALLER CALLS FOR 50-BASIS-POINT RATE HIKE IN DECEMBER

Federal Reserve Governor Christopher Waller argues the Fed should consider a 50-basis-point rate hike in December rather than splitting tightening into 25-basis-point increases in December and January.

Waller cited three consecutive 0.3% monthly core CPI readings, implying annualized inflation near 3.5%, well above the Fed's 2% target.

He warned that delaying tightening could weaken the market signal.

“My view is then you have to go 50 in December to put it in place and get it done.”

His comments reinforce expectations of a more aggressive Fed tightening cycle.

posts.name: Cullen Roche

Fun fact: The Native Americans were Capitalists, just not in the institutional sense. 

The Huron were famous for their fur trade. The Aztecs recorded merchants who bought low and sold high across mountain regions. The Yurok had shell money, private property and debt. The Wendat ran a profitable fur middleman network. The Comanche built what Pekka Hämäläinen calls an empire on horse and captive trading, and they played Spanish, French and American traders against each other, etc. 

What they mostly lacked was capital markets, not the profit motive.

posts.text:
BREAKING: A cybersecurity firm used AI to uncover a critical security flaw in Java, one of the world’s most widely used programming languages.

The bug, dubbed “Java4Shell,” was found by start-up Calif in OpenJDK, the core software that runs Java programs. Researcher Quang Luong used OpenAI’s Codex coding agent to find the flaw in about an hour, then build a working attack in about two more, for less than $200 in computing costs. Calif rated it 9.2 out of 10 for severity.

The flaw sits in Java’s Base64 decoder and can be triggered by sending just 64 “A” characters followed by a single “=.” That can corrupt the computer’s memory, potentially letting an attacker take over a server or expose sensitive data, similar to the Heartbleed bug. Calif demonstrated a working break-in on Keycloak, a widely used login system, and says tools like Jira, Confluence and Jenkins are also at risk.

Java runs at 90% of Fortune 500 companies, Calif estimates, and is used by banks, hospitals and governments worldwide. “This is such an unlikely and serious flaw,” computer scientist Toby Walsh told the BBC, because Java is designed to handle memory safely.

Oracle and OpenJDK have released fixes.

posts.name: Balaji
posts.text:
All the business school curricula need to be rewritten for the 21st century.

Good corporate governance should be defined as founder control, with dual class stock, not board control. The board is just an advisory board. The shareholder vote is a backup in the event of issues, and shareholder sales are the extreme backup.

This should be obvious from the financial performance of founder-led global tech companies vs manager-led incumbents. And also obvious in terms of just how much value these boards typically consume rather than produce.

After all, typical board members aren’t like execs that a CEO can actually assign tasks. Instead, they have power, and often time to scheme amongst themselves, but lack true operating knowledge of the underlying company. The exception is when there are real founders on the board themselves — but those are exceptions.

To be clear, the 20th century MBA-style corporate governance playbook was actually fine for the era of General Mills, General Motors, and General Electric. In that time period, the individual didn’t matter that much. They didn’t have the leverage that computers give them.

But now the Internet has obsolesced all that. So YC, Founders Fund, and a16z are much better business schools than Harvard Business School, which is culturally obsolete because it is technologically obsolete. The world it was implicitly premised on no longer exists.

However, all these intuitions and best practices, the conventions that built billion and trillion dollar companies, have only been informally advocated in blog posts and contracts. To change the defaults, we’ll need to actually write a new curriculum.

A 27% loss, yet saving is still considered safe.

UK inflation has jumped to 3.6%, the highest level in a year. The spotlight is now on the Bank of England, and markets are pricing in further rate hikes.

What usually gets lost in the noise is how inflation steadily erodes our purchasing power. Over the 16 years since the Great Financial Crisis, UK inflation has averaged 3%, or 50% above the Bank of England's official target. 

Over that same period, the average rate "offered" by UK financial institutions was just 1%. That leaves a massive gap between what your hard-earned pounds earn in a savings account and what rising prices take away.

The result is harsh: since 2011, UK savings have lost 27% of their purchasing power. Is that really what a central bank is after?

Charts like the one below are everywhere, and with government debt historically high and budget deficits uncomfortably large, the gap between yield and inflation is unlikely to close. 

Savers with the capacity and endurance should therefore look for better ways to preserve and grow their wealth. Saving is not a virtue, as the hard but objective data below show.

That is exactly why I built Prestige Investment Partners, with two distinct investment solutions focused on scarce assets and steering clear of cash and bonds.

Iraq says it has re-started oil exports via its historic Kirkuk-Ceyhan pipeline after a 12-year hiatus (Ceyhan is a Turkish port in the Mediterranean Sea).

The line inside Iraqi territory was sabotaged in 2014. At least the NVIDIA employees I spoke with really wanted him to return. The question now is whether institutional investors also decide that Jensen’s return is in their own interests. This is just factually wrong. A bank deposit is not a promise to deliver "state money". It's a promise to deliver you money. But they can explicitly refuse to deliver you cash and that's the only kind of state money you can request in the USA. 

Page 26 of Bank of America's Deposit agreement specifically says they can refuse to give you cash. 

"We may place restrictions on when and how you make large cash withdrawals. HUANG SPEAKS, THE BOARD ANSWERS

• Jensen Huang issued his first public statement since resigning as Nvidia CEO, in his own post on November 17, 2026, read in full. He said verbatim: "I did not live up to the standards expected of everyone at NVIDIA, and I have made serious mistakes in my personal life. I created problems for the Board that I deeply regret. I own my mistakes completely, and I am committed to cooperating with the Board's independent investigation."
• He thanked supporters, noted an outpouring of calls from Nvidia employees, investors, business partners and customers for him to return as CEO, and stated: "If the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO." No prior claim in the record records any public statement by Huang himself since the resignation; the comeback reporting was third party.

🚨 Anthropic’s IPO will not be just another listing. 

It will create a new public benchmark for the entire AI trade.

Here is what changes once Anthropic begins trading.

1. Software gets a public competitor for capital

A liquid company valued above $1T, generating roughly $68B in annualized revenue with approximately 900% net revenue retention, would put a daily market price on the idea that AI is taking spending from traditional application software.

IGV is already leading the market lower.

Anthropic gives investors a direct way to trade that disruption.

2. The chip impact cuts both ways

Roughly $130B in cash, plus potentially $100B in new capital, would make Anthropic one of the best-funded compute buyers in the world.

That strengthens the credibility of supplier backlogs. These commitments would be supported by cash, not merely guarantees or circular financing structures.

But Anthropic distributes its compute spending across Google TPUs, Amazon Trainium and NVIDIA GPUs.

That benefits custom silicon exposure at GOOGL and AVGO while potentially weakening NVIDIA’s pricing power.

The reported $26B of supplier stock purchases will also be viewed by some investors as vendor financing.

3. The AI scarcity premium shrinks

Until now, NVIDIA and the hyperscalers were among the only liquid ways to own the AI buildout.

That is changing.

SpaceX raised $86B in June. Anthropic is next. OpenAI is expected to follow.

Together, these companies could introduce hundreds of billions of dollars in new AI equity for the market to absorb.

That creates real competition for capital and could pressure existing AI holdings long after the IPO fundraising is complete.

4. The opening print resets the sector

Anthropic’s book is reportedly about six times oversubscribed. That demand doesn’t come from new money. It comes from funds trimming the AI names they already own.

If the debut holds, it supports private AI valuations, but it also proves investors can now own AI directly instead of through chips, cloud and software. The proxies lose their scarcity premium either way.

If the deal breaks, the pressure spreads across the full complex, especially companies whose valuations depend on continued infrastructure spending.

Suppliers get the spending in both cases. The rest of the AI complex has to absorb the new supply in both cases.

We are not predicting which outcome occurs.

But once Anthropic starts trading, the market will have a new price for AI demand, AI disruption and AI risk.

The entire complex will be valued against it.

Macro frame:

CEOs are accountable to the market, so they have to be at least somewhat honest, or else the product just doesn't work.

Modern Western politicians are typically liars, but they do need to get elected, so extremely flagrant matters sometimes lead to accountability.

Finally, journos lie for a living, but they lie in packs, all at once, together — the school-of-fish strategy — so it's hard to single one out. Who coulda knew? Therefore they have the least accountability. Their owners are also a kind of CEO, but unlike the typical CEO, their news product actually is lies and/or based-on-a-true-story.

All that is reflected here. 

Fundamentally, I submit that's what's actually going on. Most people can't keep twenty people in their head, all the journos spreading lies. But they can keep one face in their head. So they scapegoat that guy, putting all the weight on him, forgetting everyone targeting him, magnifying his faults.

It only works if he is actually important in some way, a leader who they can blame. Girardian scapegoating if you will.

THERMAL ALERT: KERCH STRAIT BRIDGE, RUSSIA

SITE
• Kerch Strait Bridge (Crimean Bridge), Russia and occupied Crimea, 19 km road-and-rail crossing of the Kerch Strait; the navigational arch span crosses the Kerch-Yenikale Canal, the main deepwater passage between the Sea of Azov and the Black Sea
• Russia's only road and rail link to Crimea and its main military logistics artery to the peninsula
• The bridge is not a refining or energy site: this analysis runs on a post by sentdefender (11/17/26 3:42 PM EDT) claiming a missile strike collapsed the arch and roadway

DETECTION
• FIRMS thermal pull over the bridge corridor (lat 45.24 to 45.37, lon 36.44 to 36.62), 11/15/26 to 11/17/26, VIIRS SNPP, NOAA-20, NOAA-21 and MODIS: zero detections
• A structural collapse with brief impact fires is a weak thermal target, so the null carries little weight either way; the event is established by wire reporting and verified imagery, not by thermal satellite
• Sentinel-2 imagery from 10/26/26 shows the arch span intact over the canal, protective booms in the water; the first clear post-event pass is still pending

CONFIDENCE
• Event real at the site: HIGH, 95%+
• Cause (Ukrainian drone and missile strike): HIGH, 90-95%
• Damage (road arch and span collapsed, road link severed; rail arch damaged, rail bridge standing): HIGH, 85-90%
• The sentdefender video as evidence of the strike: LOW, under 10%
• Rationale: claimant and target state agree on the event, and Reuters verified the imagery Kyiv published. The residual uncertainty is in the details (weapon mix, repair time), not the event. His video, by contrast, is an Exilenova+ watermarked montage set to an Eminem track; frame by frame it shows distant night explosions and one fire filmed through industrial pipe racks, a plant, not a bridge. No bridge, arch, or collapse appears in it.

CORROBORATION
• X: the primary material is Zelenskyy's own posts with video, verified by Reuters; Ukraine's General Staff stated on X that the arch and span collapsed and no vehicle can cross; sentdefender relayed the claim this afternoon, after the wires; Russian monitoring channels, via NOELreports, warn of a possible further FP-5 attack tonight
• Officials: Russia's Transport Ministry confirmed damage and suspended traffic, with rail resumed on one track today (Interfax); the Investigative Committee called it a terrorist act; Aksyonov confirmed the attack and reported two killed elsewhere in Crimea; Peskov promised a repair plan
• Web: Reuters, AP, Bloomberg News and the FT all carry the collapse, the SBU's seven-stage operation account (Palianytsia drones on the road section, Neptune and Ruta and FP-5 on the rail section, Flamingo the final blow; seven of nine missiles that hit were Ruta), and Ambrey's note that the fallen arch blocks the Kerch-Yenikale Canal; Russia's MoD claimed 1,441 drones intercepted overnight, the largest barrage of the war, and this was the second strike on the bridge in two nights
• Status: VERIFIED; road section destroyed at the arch span, rail damaged but operating on one track. Kyiv's year-plus repair estimate for the fallen roughly 6,000-tonne structure is a claimant figure, unverified

WHY IT MATTERS
• Crimea logistics: with the road link severed and rail on one track, fuel and military supply into Crimea shifts to ferries and the land corridor; Crimea fuel tightness, with retail restrictions already across six-plus Russian regions, gets worse. That supports the product-tightness side of the refining picture even as the paper crack sells off
• Azov transit: debris in the canal impairs Azov port flows (Rostov, Azov, Taganrog) days after a FIRMS-verified fire at the Azov oil depot; the campaign is now working the whole Azov-Crimea logistics chain, and a third attempt tonight is openly warned of on Russian channels
• Timing: two days before the Putin-Trump-Xi meeting in Shenzhen, a spectacular escalation that cuts against the peace-process repricing pressuring cracks this week

posts.name: IP Capital Partners
posts.text:
Existe um problema em negócios lucrativos e asset light: depois de algum tempo não há mais para onde reinvestir. O caixa se acumula e não encontra destino (a não ser o bolso do acionista). Ao longo da história da Berkshire, a companhia foi hábil em possuir dentro do seu conglomerado negócios asset light como também asset heavy, de forma que o caixa gerado num negócio mais maduro e lucrativo fosse direcionado para um com maior necessidade de emprego de capital.

A Berkshire tem, por exemplo, na See’s Candies um dos negócios mais rentáveis que já comprou: marca forte, preço premium e pouco capital empregado. O dinheiro entra e não encontra destino dentro da operação. Para um investidor comum, sobra de caixa é um bom problema. Para a Berkshire, com capital crescendo em escala, isto virou um tema a ser resolvido. Onde alocar o que a See’s não absorve?

A resposta foi a BNSF, uma ferrovia. Um negócio intensivo em capital, perene e capaz de absorver bilhões de dólares de uma só vez.

Agora troque See’s Candies por pesquisas na internet. Ben Thompson, do Stratechery, fez muito bem essa analogia. O search do Google é talvez o modelo de negócio mais perfeito já construído: custo marginal baixo, escala em todas as direções, altamente lucrativo, dominante e gerador de caixa. No entanto, com menores oportunidades para reinvestir.

Já o negócio do Google Cloud tem características distintas. Necessita de muito capital para crescer, oferece bons retornos, entretanto, inferiores ao negócio de search. Porém o mercado endereçável é potencialmente maior.

Essa combinação de negócios da Alphabet é portanto similar à lógica da Berkshire: O fluxo de caixa de negócios altamente lucrativos, asset light, é direcionado para divisões mais intensivas de uso de capital. Do search ao Google Cloud.

Um negócio extraordinário, capaz de crescer o seu valor intrínseco por décadas, não é necessariamente o mais lucrativo. É o que consegue reinvestir, em escala, o caixa que produz.

Fonte: Invest Like the Best | What Happens When the AI Boom Runs Out of Money with Ben Thompson

To decentralize AI and preserve freedom, we need a coordination layer: a market economy where agents communicate and cooperate through prices.

Teams of specialized open-weight models can outperform frontier models, just as a team of skilled people can outperform any single person. When those teams form companies, specialize, and coordinate across an entire economy, you get civilizational progress.

Coinbase is building the financial rails and accounts for the agentic economy. We’re also building the marketplace where agents can find, hire, and pay one another (see follow on post below).

Every company can now sell its own specialized open-weight model, trained on its proprietary data, that beats the frontier on narrow, high-value tasks. Builders can shop the marketplace and assemble teams of these specialized agents in minutes.

Freedom of choice and real competition in the agentic market will create far better outcomes for everyone.

(1) First, Alice Huang was at a company called Megaspeed[1], which everyone agrees bought Nvidia chips to sell to Southeast Asian companies called neoclouds. This is in itself completely legal under US law.

(2) However, some both inside and outside the admin didn't like this. They want to block Chinese nationals from accessing cloud services with Nvidia GPUs even if those servers are located outside China. Fine, but the so-called Remote Access Security Act (RASA) to block this has passed the House but not the Senate, and is not law[2].

(3) Singapore's government also looked into this when Alice Huang was on their soil[3] and didn't find any evidence that Megaspeed was actually selling chips to China illegally — let alone that she was a "Chinese spy." They did give her an entry ban, but that's like a visa denial.

(4) The related point is that it's not actually illegal to sell Nvidia chips to China! Since the Biden admin, there has been a complex and constantly-shifting set of export restrictions on chips. As of right now, Nvidia is allowed to sell H200s[4] to China, and indeed has designed these to comply with applicable law.

(5) But you know what...China actually also doesn't want Nvidia chips in China [5,6], because they want to build up their homegrown chip industry. The Nvidia chips are so good that China doesn't want to remain dependent on American chips, or vulnera

posts.name: Raoul Pal
posts.text:
Back in 2013 I was living in Spain, watching banks across southern Europe fail one after another. The European debt crisis was in full swing and it got bad enough that I bought a generator and filled the cupboards with tinned food.

Then Cyprus did something no country had done before. Its banks were going under, and instead of rescuing them, the authorities made the depositors pay... anything over €100,000 in your account was swapped for shares in a collapsing bank. They called it a bail-in. People lost their savings overnight.

That was the moment it dawned on me... you don’t actually own the money in your bank account. The bank does. And it can do what it likes with it.

So I went looking for somewhere to keep money that nobody else had a claim on, and that search led me to Bitcoin. I bought my first at around $200.

It started as my escape hatch from a broken banking system and eventually I understood it as the life raft out of the debasement trap.

It’s where the crypto chapter of The Everything Code picks the story up... with a generator and a cupboard full of tinned food.

posts.name: Nicole Perlroth
posts.text:
I haven’t lived here in awhile, but I see no other way to answer the hundreds of texts/DMs asking me if the world is, indeed, ending. 

In the span of six days, we’ve experienced;

11/12 — Microsoft outage
11/13 — Nationwide FAA ground stop
11/16 — Major US banking disruptions
11/17 — NSA’s classified internal network goes down

We need far more analysis of why so much is breaking at once. I don’t want to get out over my skis here, and what I am hearing does not contradict the messaging that most of this is the result of screwy updates. 

But stepping back, the dots are starting to form a collective picture. We are seeing: 

• An explosion in severe and critical vulnerabilities, with AI accelerating discovery to 3X the number of vulnerabilities discovered in the same period last year. This is collectively being referred to as “vulnageddon” or “the vulnpocalypse.”

• Mean time to exploit those vulnerabilities has collapsed to NEGATIVE SEVEN DAYS. AI allows attackers to find/exploit vulns far faster than software makers have time to fix them.

• Powerful AI-enabled offensive tools like ARTEX have been thrown into the hands of every third tier nation state, cybercriminal and digital arsonist, which logically creates havoc. 

• This creates enormous pressure to compress patching windows and accelerate software updates, increasing the likelihood these fixes break things in unexpected, cascading ways.

• Pressure to just “AI everything” means we are rolling out automated AI tooling on top of brittle infrastructure that can’t support it. 

My generation grew up in an extraordinary period of technological stability. We worked our way up the software stack, abstracting away layer after layer, until we lost a fundamental understanding of how the underlying systems actually work.

We were told to “move fast and break things.” VCS told us to celebrate the idea that “software would eat the world.” Now we’re telling ourselves we can simply “roll out AI” across everything, as though nothing underneath will buckle.

We never stopped to ask: SHOULD WE?

Should we be digitizing every last nook and cranny of our companies, infrastructure, healthcare, homes, cars, bodies, lives? Especially when the complexity, interdependence, and fragility we were introducing overwhelmed our ability to understand/secure/maintain the systems we built?

Nobody every asked: What if, in the name of progress, we were creating the ripest attack surface in human history?

We are now entirely dependent on software systems that almost nobody understands end to end, that increasingly few people can repair, and that attackers can now probe at machine speed. We are hearing that incident response firms, the 911 for breach victims, are backlogged six months. Even those paid on retainer lack the bandwidth to triage every incident. The cavalry is disappearing.

We are entering a period of unprecedented technological instability. 

“Software Beirut” is an incredibly apt analogy.  We are in for a period of cascading failures, whether triggered by attackers, bad updates, or our own accumulated complexity.

This, I’m sorry to say, is just the opening chapter.

posts.name: Cullen Roche
posts.text:
Fair points and I agree with much of it. Par is stabilized by state provisions. Insurance, the discount window, reserve settlement and resolution help keep a deposit at par. I’ve always described banking as a public private partnership, so no argument there. 

But backing a claim and being a claim aren’t the same thing. Your own example shows it. A purchase and assumption gives the depositor a liability of another bank. The state guarantees the deposit’s par value and settles it as a deposit. SVB proves the point. Uninsured depositors had no claim on the state. It took a discretionary systemic risk exception to make them whole, and they were made whole as deposits. If deposits were claims on state money, that exception wouldn’t have been necessary.

Bank holdings of Treasuries and MBS are state debt on the bank’s asset side. They tell you how good the deposit is, not what it’s a claim on. The depositor’s contract ends at the bank. Read any deposit agreement. It’s a dollar denominated debt, guaranteed and supported by the state, and paid in whatever form the bank chooses.

Numerous people in this thread keep saying deposits are a "claim" on state money. They obviously never read their deposit agreement because nowhere in those documents does the bank guarantee to deliver you state money. In fact, they say the exact opposite. Bank of Americas 2026 deposit agreement makes this explicit:

"we may refuse to honot your request [for cash] if you do not comply with these restrictions, or if we believe that honoring that request to withdraw cash would cause an undue hardship or security risk". 

That's about as crystal clear as it gets. BofA is not obligated to give you cash and they cannot give you reserves. Your deposit is a claim on whatever the bank deems reasonable. You have a claim on bank deposits, not state money. 

So MMT's entire narrative blows up on this one concept and all you had to do to understand it was read the fine print in the document every banking customer gets. Deposits aren't some vertical claim on horizontal monies and MMT is spreading a certifiable falsehood by saying so.

posts.name: James E. Thorne
posts.text:
Governor Waller’s Shock Therapy Is Malpractice

Fed Governor Christopher Waller wants to “shock people.” Before he does, he should look at a chart.
His evidence that inflation is “spreading” is that about 70% of core services are running above 3%. That isn’t a crisis. It’s normal. Since 1968, core services CPI has averaged 4.77% and has been above 2% in 94.6% of months. Since 2010, including a decade of zero rates and quantitative easing, it has averaged 3.09%. September’s reading was 3.2%. 

Waller is sounding the alarm over a number that sits almost exactly on its 16-year average.

Rate hikes have never fixed it. Services inflation fell below 2% only three times in 58 years: 1983, 2010 and 2021. Each took a deep recession: Volcker, the global financial crisis and the pandemic. The steepest hiking cycle in four decades left it at 3.2%. So when Waller says Americans need a “shock,” he means a recession. He should say so.

Alan Blinder explained this in 1982. Energy shocks are special factors that fade; the baseline moves slowly. The energy shock is fading now: Brent is down 33%, crack spreads 36% and gasoline 16%, and the war spike falls out of CPI in March. Waller wants to tighten right into the disinflation.

His own words undercut him. He concedes market expectations “have not risen.” The 5y5y is at 2.15%, below average. What’s left is that firms might pass on 3%, and “I just heard someone last week.” A Fed governor is proposing to reverse 75bp of cuts, and possibly more, on the basis of an anecdote.

This isn’t vigilance. It’s malpractice. A central banker who would trigger a recession to move a number that has been above 2% for six decades has lost the plot. Enough is enough. Governor Waller should go.

posts.name: James E. Thorne
posts.text:
Enough Is Enough: Governor Waller Should Go!

Fed Governor Christopher Waller told CNBC this morning that the Fed needs to reverse all three of last year’s quarter-point cuts and “may need to do more.” “If you really want to get it down, you’ve got to start taking more aggressive actions,” he said.

Where is the data?

The inflation scare is an energy shock, and it’s unwinding. Brent is down 33% from its April peak. Crack spreads are down 36% since October, supertanker rates 24% and retail gasoline 16%. Iraq has reopened the Kirkuk-Ceyhan pipeline, so oil can flow around Hormuz. The glut has reached refiners and is moving to the pump.

The war spike drops out of year-over-year CPI in March. If gasoline holds at today’s price, headline inflation falls from about 3.6% in January to about 2.8% in March and close to 2% by May. 

Waller wants to tighten aggressively right into that.

Expectations aren’t moving. The 5y5y is at 2.15%, below its long-run average. Wages aren’t driving inflation; even the Fed’s most hawkish regional president, Alberto Musalem, concedes the labour market “has not yet been a driver of inflation.” Rate hikes can’t refill a tanker or reopen a strait.

The math makes it worse. As inflation falls, real rates rise on their own. Reversing 75bp and “more” on top of that would tighten twice into a disinflation, and the people who pay are households, small businesses and anyone with a floating-rate mortgage.

A governor who calls for aggressive tightening while every leading price signal points down isn’t guarding price stability. He’s creating instability. This is irresponsible, and Governor Waller should step aside.

The European Central Bank will discuss raising banks' minimum reserve requirements from 1% to 2% on November 25, Reuters reports.

The move would require lenders to hold more non-interest-bearing reserves, saving euro-area central banks approximately €4.4 billion annually while withdrawing liquidity from the financial system.

A decision could be delayed until December 17.

The change would reduce central-bank losses but could pressure commercial bank profitability and lending capacity.

posts.name: Cullen Roche
posts.text:
Legally, reserves are liabilities of the 12 Federal Reserve Banks, which are federally chartered corporations with member bank shareholders. They aren't liabilities of the Treasury or of "the State."

Congress drew this line itself. Section 16 of the Federal Reserve Act makes Fed notes obligations of the United States. Reserves never got that language. Courts have treated the Reserve Banks as independent corporations too, not federal agencies (Lewis v. United States, 9th Cir. 1982).

posts.name: Cullen Roche
posts.text:
The reserves part is wrong. A depositor has no claim on reserves. Reserves are the bank's asset sitting at the Fed, and a depositor is an unsecured creditor of the bank. I can tell my bank to pay you. I can't tell it to move reserves. How my bank squares up with your bank is its business, whether that's reserves, netting, a correspondent balance or an overnight loan.

And you don't get reserves either. You get a deposit at your bank. That's where the payment ends for both of us. UCC 4A is explicit about this. My payment to you is complete when your bank accepts the payment order, and my debt is discharged at that point. If your bank accepted before it got paid and my bank then blows up, that's your bank's loss, not mine and not yours.

So there are two settlements here. Customers settle in deposits. Banks settle with each other in reserves, or net down until there's a residual they settle in reserves. Same bank payments don't touch reserves at all. Reserves are the final settlement asset between banks. They aren't how customer payments get settled. So you literally cannot demand state money.

You keep saying that I only rises when C falls. That is simply not true. You are confusing increases and reductions in the nominal amounts of GDP components with increases and reductions in their shares of GDP.

To the extent that structural transfers that shift income from households to subsidize investment lower the household income and consumption shares of GDP, the combined share of investment and net exports must rise. There is no way around this. If nominal consumption rises less quickly than nominal investment and net exports rise, however, the only way to balance it is with slower growth in production, in which case investment and net exports can decline even as their shares of GDP rise.

More oil amateur hour from @DrJStrategy 

He sees a 36% drop in crack spreads and declares an oil glut.

A 3-2-1 crack spread measures refining margins, not crude supply-demand balance.

quoted.text:
Crack Spreads Are Dropping Like a Stone

The US 3-2-1 crack spread, the refiner’s margin for turning crude into gasoline and diesel, has collapsed 36% in six weeks, from $ 65.56 a barrel on 9 October to $ 41.90 today. It’s at a new low and still falling.

That tells you the glut has moved downstream. Fat margins pulled refiners into running flat out, and now product markets are swamped. Gasoline and diesel prices are falling faster than crude. That’s exactly what wholesale RBOB futures, down 20%, and $ 3.78 at the pump were already signalling.

Collapsing margins also mean more relief is coming. Retail prices lag wholesale by weeks, so the pump hasn’t finished falling. Every 10 cents off gasoline takes about 9bp off headline CPI. November is shaping up for a negative headline print, and in March the war spike drops out of the year-over-year math.

This is a supply glut, not a demand problem, and it’s doing the Fed’s job for it. Hiking 1% into a collapsing refining margin isn’t vigilance. It’s insanity.

Paul Tudor Jones: I Went Broke Three Times, Now I Focus on What I Can Lose

In the past two weeks, we've been playing as big as we've ever played before, because of the fact we think we know what's going on. Like right now, I'm watching the currencies, I'm watching crude, I'm watching stocks and bonds. They're all interrelated. The whole world is simply nothing but a big flowchart for capital. And if I start getting hurt in, for instance, stocks or bonds, then I'm going to make a total portfolio adjustment just because of the fact I might not like the way the numbers are going over the course of the day.

I've personally gone bankrupt, not declared bankruptcy, but lost everything I had and had to borrow from friends three times in nine years that I've been in the business, where I'd go sit in the park and just sit there and just go, "I can't believe this. You know, this is the end. This is the end of my life."

Where you want to be is always in control, never wishing, always trading, and always first and foremost protecting your ass. That's why most people lose money as individual investors or as traders, because of the fact they're not focusing on losing money. They need to focus on the money that they have at risk. How much capital is at risk in any single investment they have? If everyone spent 90% of their time on that, or the 90% of their time on pie-in-the-sky ideas about how much money they're going to make, then they'd be incredibly successful investors.

You misunderstand how bank lending can add to NFA. For example:

A firm borrows $100k to invest and pays it out as wages and dividends. Households end up with $100k in deposits and no debt, a $100k gain in net financial assets. The business sector carries the matching debt but owns a new productive asset. No government deficit needed. Household NFA is created whenever another sector runs a deficit, and businesses borrowing to invest is the main way that happens in a healthy economy. This has an even larger multiplier on househokd net wealth if firms are revalued higher.

The fact that taxes settle in the reserve system doesn't change the fact that the entire system is structured to service bank deposit redistribution.

quoted.text:
We will stop measles outbreaks, protect American families, and work to regain U.S. measles elimination status. I continue to recommend MMR vaccination as the most effective way to prevent measles.

Worldwide COVID-era disruptions interrupted routine childhood vaccination, leaving gaps in protection here and abroad. The multi-year global outbreak has caused many nations to lose their elimination status including, Armenia, Austria, Azerbaijan, Bolivia, Canada, Mexico, Spain, United Kingdom, and Uzbekistan.

Under Dr. Schwartz’s leadership, CDC has provided approximately $100 million in additional funding since August to strengthen prevention and response to measles and other vaccine-preventable diseases.

CDC has worked alongside state teams in Texas, South Carolina, Virginia, Kansas, New Mexico, and Wisconsin to help bring their outbreaks rapidly and successfully under control. CDC is also supporting Pennsylvania and New York with epidemiologists and other experts.

We are working to close vaccination gaps and rebuild public trust. We will answer families’ questions honestly about vaccine benefits and risks and work with trusted health care providers and community leaders to prevent measles, limit its spread, and support timely treatment.

We will support Americans who become ill, regardless of vaccination status, and for the first time equip health care providers with guidance to diagnose and treat measles and its complications.
